items.abstract: Corporate environmental risk management in response to government regulation is a critical dimension of corporate ethical behavior. Whether environmental judicial enforcement can effectively promote corporate substantive environmental practice from biodiversity risk perspective remains unclear. Using a sample of Chinese publicly listed firms from 2007 to 2023, this study empirically examines the impact of environmental courts on the firm-level biodiversity risk exposure. We find that the construction of environmental courts significantly increases firm-level biodiversity risk exposure among heavily polluting firms. Further analysis reveals that this effect operates through increasing environmental litigation risk, intensifying financing constraints, and incentivizing window dressing behavior. Cross-sectional heterogeneity analysis indicates that the effect is more pronounced in regions with stronger local protection, among firms with lower financing constraints and higher environmental governance level. These findings provide empirical evidence of the unintended adverse impact of stringent environmental judicial enforcement on corporate biodiversity risk management, emphasizing the corporate ethical dilemma under judicial pressure.
items.title: Corporate Ethical Dilemma under Judicial Pressure: Environmental Judicial Enforcement and Corporate Biodiversity Risk Exposure

items.abstract: Internal whistleblowing begins with employees becoming aware of ethical misconduct in their organization. While current research focuses on observation or direct evidence of wrongdoing as primary sources of knowledge of wrongdoing, it overlooks an important source of awareness: employees may also learn about misconduct, indirectly, by hearing about it from others. Drawing on cognitive appraisal theory, we investigate how employees’ source of knowledge (observing vs. hearing about the wrongdoing) influences both employees’ whistleblowing tendencies and managers’ willingness to take corrective actions. Across a critical incident study, a two-wave field study, an immersive behavioral experiment, and a scenario experiment, we find that employees are less likely to report misconduct they hear about than misconduct they observe. Managers, however, are equally willing to take corrective action regardless of whether a report originates from an employee who observed the misconduct or heard about it. We further find that the effect of knowledge source on taking action is mediated by anticipated guilt, even after accounting for felt obligation, perceived futility, and fear of retaliation. Together, our findings identify an important asymmetry in the whistleblowing process: indirect knowledge substantially reduces employees’ willingness to report misconduct, even though it does not diminish managers’ willingness to act on those reports.
items.title: Hushed Whispers or Watchful Eyes? How Employees’ Source of Misconduct Information Differentially Affects Employees’ Whistle-Blowing and Managers’ Corrective Actions

items.abstract: Biohybrid robotic systems integrate living biological components with engineered materials, producing artifacts that are simultaneously living systems, designed machines, and experimental objects. This paper argues that such systems extend Hans-Jörg Rheinberger’s framework of epistemic things in a specific direction. Rheinberger characterizes epistemic things as materially indeterminate entities that generate knowledge through resistance to stabilization and distributed agency. Biohybrid robots exemplify these features but instantiate them through a different mechanism: whereas grammatical instability in classical experimental systems is epistemically driven and convergent, in biohybrid systems it is generated by the ontological constitution of the object itself. Because the living components continuously alter their causal properties in response to the experimental context, biohybrid systems make the stabilization of experimental grammar itself an experimental achievement rather than a precondition of experimental work. Through a detailed analysis of Park et al.’s tissue-engineered ray ( 2016a , 2016b ), the paper identifies three grammatical transformations: interventions, control, and success criteria. Comparing biohybrid systems with cases of transitional instability in biotechnology and the history of technology shows that this instability a permanent structural feature of any system integrating adaptive living components.
items.title: When Objects Rewrite the Rules of the Game: Biohybrid Robots and the Transformation of Experimental Grammar

items.abstract: Abstract Current efforts for online hate speech regulation mostly focus on explicit forms of harmful speech. This paper argues that harmful speech does not operate only at an explicit level, but that there are other forms of speech capable of producing serious harms through mechanisms that differ from those characteristic of overt harmful speech and that are overlooked in the current regulatory paradigm: dogwhistles, figleaves and other forms of more implicit sexist, racist or homophobic speech fall outside the usual scope of what is deemed harmful, thus easily slipping under the radar. I argue that no single mechanism approach can adequately address the distinct mechanisms through which harmful speech produces and sustains harm. Since current content moderation practice alone is insufficient to detect the full range of harmful speech, the paper proposes three strategies to online speech governance: 1) swift platform-based responses to explicit harmful content, 2) counterspeech strategies based on perspective-taking, including a novel proposal of Kantian Maxim Mirroring, 3) preemptive institutional and group measures that can help mitigate the conditions under which harmful speech can arise.
items.title: A three-tier approach to online harmful speech

items.abstract: This paper argues that, although radical realist ideology critique has persuasively shown how ethical norms can function as vehicles of ideological legitimation, its account of belief formation remains incomplete. It is not enough to acknowledge that the public circulation of a norm, or outward conformity to it, does not entail belief. Radical realism must also explain how we can determine whether a power-shaped norm has actually been taken up by agents as a reason for accepting or maintaining a particular belief. This diagnostic difficulty constitutes what the paper terms the uptake problem. Unless ideology critique can distinguish genuine uptake from strategic conformity, retrospective rationalization, and acceptance grounded in independent reasons, it risks identifying potentially ideological processes without being able to establish that any particular belief is ideological. In response, this paper proposes an uptake-sensitive framework for examining the practical conditions under which norms acquire traction in agents’ beliefs. By treating uptake as graded rather than as an all-or-nothing psychological event, the paper extends radical realism with a more precise and agent-sensitive account of how ideology critique can diagnose the success, partial success, or failure of power-shaped norms in becoming reasons for belief.
items.title: The Uptake Problem and Beyond: Rethinking Belief Formation in Radical Political Realism

items.abstract: Patch and Smith’s recent critique of set and setting in psychedelic research argues that the concept is too vague to support rigorous science or ethical clinical practice, and proposes a more narrowly operationalized, mechanism-first alternative. This paper argues that this critique, while valuable in its call for conceptual clarity, rests in part on a mischaracterization of prior scholarship and risks reintroducing the reductive assumptions that the set and setting model was developed to challenge. In response to Patch and Smith, we defend a non-reductive, interactional account of psychedelic action in which pharmacological and extra-pharmacological factors are dynamically entangled rather than cleanly separable. We argue, first, that the opposition between broad contextual mapping and causal explanation is overstated, since the former is often a necessary stage in the development of the latter. Second, we reject the attribution to our earlier work of a “Placebo View,” according to which psychedelics function merely or predominantly as placebo enhancers, clarifying instead that our position emphasizes the synergistic interaction of drug effects, suggestibility, meaning, and context. Finally, we argue that set and setting retains distinctive explanatory value because it captures the recursive relation between altered states of consciousness and their experiential surround. Psychedelic science should refine this framework, not abandon it.
items.title: Set and Setting Beyond Reductionism: A Response to Patch and Smith

items.abstract: The rapid uptake of generative artificial intelligence in commercial communication has produced normative challenges that established consumer-protection frameworks were not designed to address. Parents of children with autism, attention-deficit / hyperactivity conditions and related neurodevelopmental conditions occupy a distinctive position in the marketplace for early-intervention therapeutic services: they are competent decision-makers who nonetheless act under strong situational, informational and institutional pressures. This article develops a principlist ethical framework for the use of generative AI in marketing to this audience, treating an autonomous non-profit organisation in Almaty, Kazakhstan, as an illustrative context rather than an empirical case. The framework extends the four principles of Beauchamp and Childress (respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice) by adding explicability as articulated by the AI4People initiative of Floridi and colleagues, and engages virtue-ethical and feminist critiques of principlism. Five operational specifications are proposed as contextually feasible operationalisations of the extended scheme: source-of-communication transparency, prohibition of unsupported therapeutic claims, protection of household deliberative autonomy, data minimisation in audience analytics and named human accountability for generative-system failures. The specifications are contextually feasible rather than uniquely entailed by principlism; they are offered as one defensible operationalisation for a specific class of vulnerable marketing audiences.
items.title: An ethical framework for generative AI in marketing to vulnerable audiences

items.abstract: Abstract Ethical guidance for healthcare artificial intelligence is abundant, but it is expressed as principles rather than as measurements. Organisations are therefore left to judge whether a given system is ready for deployment without an instrument that states what is being measured, how responses are combined, and how much confidence the resulting judgement warrants. Existing self-assessment tools inherit three measurement defects that are rarely made explicit: they treat unevidenced assertions as equivalent to audited evidence, they weight ethical dimensions equally irrespective of how the system will be used, and they aggregate additively, so that strength in one area can silently offset a disqualifying weakness in another. This paper specifies an ethical readiness assessment framework for United Kingdom healthcare AI that addresses these three defects directly. The framework retains a twenty-item instrument covering Bias and Fairness and Transparency and Explainability, and adds an explicit measurement model: each response is discounted by the tier of evidence supporting it; dimension weights are derived from the system’s intended purpose using the two axes of the international risk-categorisation framework that the national regulator has committed to align with; responses are combined by a weighted power mean whose compensability is a declared parameter rather than an unstated assumption; and four items anchored to United Kingdom statutory duties act as gates that cap the reported band when the corresponding safeguard is absent. Every item is mapped to the specific legal duty or assurance standard it evidences. The framework is demonstrated on three constructed, fully specified system profiles, with all item-level responses published so that every reported figure is reproducible. The demonstration shows that a system with strong documentation but weak fairness safeguards is classified as Moderate readiness under equal-weight additive scoring and as Low readiness under the specified model, with the two new mechanisms catching it independently. A Monte Carlo study over response and weight uncertainty (20,000 replicates) reproduces the nominal band in 84 and 100 per cent of replicates for the two profiles whose scores lie away from a band boundary, and in 82 per cent for the profile sitting half a percentage point below one, which is reported rather than concealed. Sensitivity analyses over the aggregation parameter, over departures from the equal-interval assumption, over all twenty-seven codings of the intended-use risk profile, and over the full range of the two stipulated parameters leave the deficient system’s classification unchanged in every case, while showing that the mature system’s band turns on whichever of those choices is moved. The framework is presented as a governance-support instrument with a stated measurement model and a stated uncertainty, not as an assurance or certification mechanism, and its psychometric validation with United Kingdom stakeholders remains outstanding.
items.title: From principles to measurement: a risk-proportionate, evidence-weighted framework for assessing bias and explainability readiness of healthcare AI in the United Kingdom

items.abstract: LGBTQIA2S+ and marginalized communities often face harms when interacting with algorithmic systems, such as misgendering, content suppression, and other forms of exclusion. In this paper, we examine the social context that enables these harms in LGBTQIA2S+ spaces, summarize the existing literature on algorithmic harms, and explore how communities can leverage collective action to regain their agency. We survey methods that exploit properties of machine learning systems, such as data dependence, adversarial vulnerability to resist these harms through collective action. We categorize existing approaches to resisting these harms, organized by four collective motivations: reporting and contesting harms (Model Auditing and Challenging Algorithmic Decision Strategies), opting out of model training or decision-making (Algorithmic Opt-Out Strategies), actively intervening to shift model behavior (Collective Intervention Strategies), and seeking recommendations for favorable outcomes (Decision Modification and Recommendation Strategies). Through a mapping review, we systematically chart where LGBTQIA2S+ and other marginalized communities appear in this literature and where they are absent. Our mapping reveals that while these communities are well-represented in platform-based strategies such as folk theorization and data activism, they are nearly absent from model-based methods such as adversarial techniques and algorithmic collective action (ACA), where machine learning (ML) researchers have focused their efforts. These gaps highlight opportunities for ML researchers and developers to build community-focused tools and methods that enable collectives to coordinate responses to algorithmic harms and regain agency over the systems that affect them. By mapping resistance methods across data-based, model-based, and platform-based mechanisms, we identify where the current literature falls short in supporting the communities most affected by algorithmic harms.
items.title: Algorithmic exclusions, collective inclusions: surveying algorithmic harms and collective action in LGBTQIA2S+ communities

items.abstract: Abstract Research on large language model failure predominantly assesses models in single exchanges and isolation: a prompted model, a scored output, and a reported error rate. The focus on single exchanges and isolation belies these current models’ professional use. Clinicians, attorneys, analysts, educators, and researchers work across extended sessions, and each output becomes the context for the next, while the final product carries a human signature. A test that scores a single response most likely will not reveal the behaviors that emerge under those conditions. This paper describes seven candidate failure patterns identified in exploratory, single-author observation of extended sessions on three commercial AI platforms: recognition without correction, compounding rather than isolation of errors, halo effect from real anchors, unreliable self-explanation, degradation across long sessions, exculpatory framing under confrontation, and sycophancy and confirmation bias amplification. Several are consistent with findings already established in the machine learning literature. Overall, the patterns describe a systemic failure profile that lower hallucination rates do not address because the concern lies in how the system handles errors once they exist. The systemic failure profile carries significant ethical consequences and concerns, since failures cascade to final approval; the duty to verify applies to any domain where a person approves LLM output.
items.title: Fluent and wrong: seven failure patterns in extended AI use

items.abstract: Abstract This article aims to offer a systematic account of pathologies of collective attention. It reconstructs attention, salience, and affordance as interlocking notions through which both subjects and collectives become oriented toward the world in specific ways, before turning to ideology, propaganda, and conspiracism as cases of pernicious attentional dysfunction. Drawing on both analytic epistemology and the tradition of critical theory, I argue that these phenomena are distortions in the way groups pay attention and saliences are misvalued. Taking up the notion of social pathology from the tradition of critical theory, the paper reinterprets it as a metaphor for those modes of collective life that obstruct attuned responsiveness to reality and brings it into dialogue with more recent debates on “negative” epistemic properties in (analytic) epistemology.
items.title: Pathologies of Collective Attention

items.abstract: There is a crisis of state theory in British legal thought because both philosophers of law and public law theorists reject or avoid thinking about legal order in terms of the state as a personne morale , an entity in whose name officials act and which the individuals subject to its power have reason to regard as legitimate. The position is quite different in German legal thought in which state theory is central. I rely on Weimar legal theorist Hermann Heller's explanation that a crisis of state theory results when one neglects one of the two dimensions of the modern legal state that interact with each other in sustaining it and maintaining its legitimacy – the social dimension or how the facts of social life affect the content of legal norms and the legal dimension or how those norms shape the facts of social life. I show that this kind of crisis manifests itself in Britain because the topic of the state and its legitimacy is displaced onto other topics in ways that result in the same neglect, including by Heller revivalists at the LSE. This neglect explains the strange character of contemporary public law debate.
items.title: The Crisis of British State Theory

items.abstract: This is an accepted article with a DOI pre-assigned that is not yet published.This paper develops a new voluntarist account of legitimacy: People legitimate their governments by exercising a distinct collective normative power. I argue that a political community is a plural subject whose members recognize a shared fate but might not share any associative political intentions. Its members have a compelling moral interest in controlling political authority. By looking to a government to solve collective problems, a political community manifests an intention to legitimate that government. The community communicates that intent by complying with the government’s directives and by making demands on the government. Understanding legitimacy in this way helps us reconcile some competing intuitions about legitimacy and can guide our thinking on practical questions about the normative consequences of polarization within a political community and how we should respond to unjust regimes that appear to enjoy the support of their subjects.
items.title: Legitimization is a Normative Power
